observations.statement: Defines the estimand as the ratio of the jump in the outcome's conditional expectation to the jump in treatment probability at the cutoff, following the standard fuzzy-RD local-average-treatment-effect interpretation under continuity and monotonicity.
observations.quote: local average treatment effect among units at the cutoff

observations.statement: States identification through a formal Holder-type smoothness class with a bounded second derivative on each side of the cutoff, rather than through a continuity-of-density argument, and treats both point and partial identification as covered by the same construction.

Frames two specific threats to conventional fuzzy-RD inference, running variables with discrete or otherwise irregular support, and weak identification when the treatment-probability jump is small, as the motivation for the proposed method.

Supports the practical relevance of the threats it discusses by reporting in the opening footnote a survey of fuzzy-RD applications across several years in five top economics journals, classified by irregular support and by strength of the first stage.

The empirical illustration reuses a household survey sample assembled by combining several waves of a national income and wealth survey over a roughly decade-long period, originally compiled for an earlier published retirement-consumption study rather than newly collected for this paper.

States the unit of observation as the individual survey respondent, with the running variable measured in years from an age-based retirement-eligibility threshold, and reports the total number of individuals in a table note rather than in the main narrative.
Defines the outcome as the natural logarithm of total household spending, a standard log transformation rather than a level or index measure.

Defines treatment as an indicator for being retired and the running variable as years from the formal retirement-eligibility threshold, explicitly noting that this running variable is discrete even though it has fairly rich support.

Constructs its key tuning parameters, smoothness bounds on the curvature of the outcome and treatment conditional-expectation functions, from two competing rule-of-thumb formulas based on fitting global polynomial specifications to the data by least squares.

Reports each method's confidence set in the main comparison table as a midpoint and half-length pair, stated explicitly as a choice made to ease comparing the location and length of different intervals side by side.
The comparison table's note gives the total number of data points and the nominal coverage level used for all confidence sets, rather than repeating sample size separately for each row or column.

Because the confidence sets require researcher-chosen curvature bounds rather than resting on a clustering or robust-variance assumption, justifies inference by recommending a sensitivity analysis across a range of plausible bound values plus estimated one-sided bounds to guard against overly optimistic choices.

States independent and identically distributed sampling as a formal assumption underlying its coverage theorem, and notes in passing that this could be weakened to accommodate certain forms of dependent sampling such as cluster sampling, without implementing that extension.

Justifies departing from the standard nearest-neighbor variance estimator commonly recommended in the RD literature by showing it is not uniformly valid over the assumed smoothness class, and proposes a replacement based on a local best-linear predictor instead of a local sample average.

Reports confidence sets under two different rule-of-thumb smoothness-bound choices side by side in the main comparison table, functioning as a form of tuning-parameter sensitivity check for the bandwidth-like curvature bound.

The raw-data figure's second panel plots the empirical share of treated individuals against the running variable, visually displaying the treatment-probability discontinuity on which identification of the fuzzy design rests.

Treats the strength of identification, the size of the treatment-probability jump, as a design parameter that is deliberately varied across simulated data-generating processes and explicitly linked to the reliability of the different confidence-set constructions.

Systematically compares the proposed confidence set against seven alternative constructions that differ in bias-handling strategy and bandwidth rule, crossed with both an Anderson-Rubin-type and a delta-method construction, and summarizes all comparisons in one large simulation table.

Examines robustness to the researcher-chosen smoothness bounds by comparing coverage under the true bounds, twice the true bounds, and half the true bounds, alongside two rule-of-thumb estimators of those bounds.

Summarizes power-like behavior away from the true parameter value in a single multi-panel figure comparing all method variants for one representative simulation design, rather than reporting a separate power table.

Points repeatedly to a separate online supplemental appendix for additional robustness results, including a variant using an alternative point estimator and further data-generating-process combinations, rather than including them in the main text.
observations.locator: Footnotes 12 and 14, referencing Supplemental Appendices E and F

observations.statement: Interprets differences across methods in purely relative terms, comparing the location and length of confidence sets against one another and against global-parametric alternatives, rather than benchmarking any single estimate against a sample mean or external reference value.

Notes that the two global parametric benchmarks are the only methods whose confidence sets exclude zero, but attributes this to their vulnerability to model-misspecification bias rather than treating it as more credible evidence of a nonzero effect.

Flags that one of the three simulated curvature settings, constructed to have very high curvature near the cutoff, may not correspond to a realistic empirical scenario, cautioning against over-generalizing results from that setting.

Warns that a commonly used fourth-order-polynomial rule of thumb for the smoothness bound can produce erratic overfits that vastly overstate the true curvature bound, and recommends always checking the polynomial fit before trusting that shortcut.

The post-references editorial note discloses that the journal's reproducibility check ran on a simplified version of the code because the paper's simulation algorithms were judged too computationally demanding to rerun in full.

Opens the empirical section with a two-panel raw-data figure showing average outcome and treatment share against the running variable, with the size of each plotted point scaled by the number of underlying observations at that value.

Because the reported outputs are confidence sets rather than point estimates with hypothesis tests, none of the result tables use significance stars; intervals are simply reported as ranges or as midpoint-plus-half-length pairs.
Table notes state the number of underlying data points and the nominal coverage level of the reported confidence sets, functioning as the paper's equivalent of a standard-error or sample-size note.
observations.locator: Table I and Table II notes

observations.statement: Develops the estimand, the proposed confidence-set construction, and its theoretical coverage and shape properties before presenting any empirical illustration or simulation evidence, and defers all formal proofs to a dedicated appendix.

The introduction's second paragraph states the paper's contribution directly and previews its two main theoretical results, correct coverage under weak conditions and asymptotic equivalence to existing methods in canonical settings, before the formal setup section begins.

Places the comparison with the standard delta-method approach and a later practical-implementation discussion in their own numbered sections after the core method is derived, separating the proposal itself from why it differs from existing practice and how to implement it.

A post-references editorial note states that the replication package is hosted at a cited repository and that the journal checked the included data and code for their ability to reproduce the paper's results before approving the online appendices.

States that all computations are carried out in R, with the authors' own bias-aware routines built on one named package and the comparison confidence intervals computed using functions from a second named package.

Describes the empirical dataset only by reference to the earlier published study that assembled it, without independently documenting the survey's access procedure, restrictions, or institutional source in this paper.

Frames the proposed construction as covering both point-identified canonical settings and partially identified settings with the same procedure, so that researchers do not need to pre-judge which identification regime applies to their data before choosing a method.

concordance.paper_says: Proposes a bias-aware Anderson-Rubin-type confidence set built on local linear SRD-type regression as its main proposed method (Section 3).
concordance.card_shows: Design d1 (variant bias_aware_anderson_rubin) is implemented via spec s1, RDHonest:::NPRHonest.fit with sclass='H', opt.criterion='FLCI', se.method='supplied.var'.

concordance.paper_says: Uses bias-aware delta-method confidence intervals as a comparison benchmark to the proposed Anderson-Rubin construction (Section 5).
concordance.card_shows: Design d2 (variant delta_method) is implemented via spec s2, the same RDHonest:::NPRHonest.fit routine applied to the delta-method auxiliary statistic.

concordance.paper_says: Reports a robust bias correction delta-method confidence interval, computed with the rdrobust package, as one of the comparison methods in the empirical application table.
concordance.card_shows: Spec s3 calls rdrobust::rdrobust(vce='nn') under design d1, matching a local-polynomial delta-method comparison estimator.

concordance.paper_says: States that variants using the optimized RD estimator of Imbens and Wager (2019) in place of local linear regression are reported in a supplemental appendix rather than the main text.
concordance.card_shows: Design d3 (variant optimized_rd) is implemented via spec s5, an optrdd2 call, consistent with the paper's optimized-RD variant.

gaps: No heterogeneous-effects or subgroup analysis is reported anywhere in the paper; it is a methods paper with a single illustrative empirical application.
No mechanism evidence or intermediate-outcome analysis is presented; the retirement-consumption application illustrates the inference method rather than investigating why the effect occurs.
No preregistration, IRB approval, or research-ethics statement is mentioned.
No manipulation or density test (e.g. McCrary-type) of the running variable is reported for the empirical application, even though the running variable is discrete.
The introduction has no explicit 'the paper proceeds as follows' roadmap paragraph; the structure must be inferred from the numbered section headings.

No cluster-robust standard errors are implemented or discussed in the empirical application, although a footnote on the i.i.d. sampling assumption notes it could be weakened to allow cluster sampling.
Beyond naming the R packages used (RDHonest, rdrobust, optrdd, FRD, foreach, xtable, tikzDevice, abind), no software version numbers or a session/environment record are reported in the main text.

reading.note: All 25 pages were read: introduction, setup/estimand, the bias-aware Anderson-Rubin construction, theoretical-properties section, the delta-method comparison, the implementation section (standard errors, bandwidth choice, smoothness bounds, regression-kink extension), the empirical application and simulation study, the appendix proofs of Theorems 1-3, the reference list, and the post-references editorial/replication note. The appendix proofs (pages 16-24) were read for their stated assumptions, structure and conclusions rather than verified line by line, since this note records reporting and inference practice, not mathematical correctness. The paper's Supplemental Appendices A-F, cited repeatedly for additional proofs, robustness variants (e.g. the optimized-RD estimator) and extra simulation designs, are a separate online document not included in this text extraction and were not read.
